NOS. 25-238, 25-566
CUTBERTO VIRAMONTES, ET AL., PETITIONERS
v.

EDDIE GRANT, JR., ET AL., PETITIONERS,

TO THE UNITED STATES COURTS OF APPEALS
FOR THE SEVENTH AND SECOND CIRCUITS

BRIEF FOR LUKE SMITH MORGAN AND JACOB
D. CHARLES  AS AMICI CURIAE IN SUPPORT
OF RESPONDENTS

INTEREST OF AMICI ∗
Amici curiae are constitutional law scholars who
have written extensively on the Second Amendment and

∗ All parties have been informed of the filing of this amici curiae
brief.  No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and no person or entity, other than amici curiae or their counsel made a monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation
or submission of this brief.

2



firearms law.  Their scholarship has been published in
leading law journals and cited by courts across the country.  Amici have studied Second Amendment doctrine’s
relation to other constitutional-rights doctrines and
closely followed judicial decisions applying New York
State Rifle & Pistol Association  v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1
(2022).  They are well situated to explain how the Second
Amendment framework fits into the constellation of individual-rights adjudication and the risks that may arise
without this Court’s clarifications.
Jacob D. Charles is an Associate Professor of Law
at Pepperdine University Caruso School of Law.  His
scholarship focuses on Second Amendment doctrine and
theory.  He is the co-author of a leading Second Amendment casebook, The Second Amendment: Gun Rights
And Regulation (Foundation Press, 2025).  His scholarship has appeared or is forthcoming in the Harvard Law
Review Forum, Columbia Law Review, University of
Chicago Law Review, Virginia Law Review, Duke Law
Journal, and others.  See, e.g., Bruen’s Tenth Amendment Problem, 93 U. Chi. L. Rev. (forthcoming 2027)
(with Jonah Gelbach); Ancillary Rights, 173 U. Penn. L.
Rev. 1269 (2025); The Dead Hand of a Silent Past: Bruen,
Gun Rights, and the Shackles of History, 73 Duke L.J.
67 (2023); Violence and Nondelegation, 135 Harv. L.
Rev. F. 463 (2022) (with Darre ll A. H. Miller); Securing
Gun Rights by Statute: The Right to Keep and Bear
Arms Outside the Constituti on, 120 Mich. L. Rev. 581
(2022).
Luke Smith Morgan is an Assistant Professor of
Law at Campbell University Norman Adrian Wiggins
School of Law, with teac hing focused on public law
courses including civil procedure, federal courts, and

3



constitutional law.  His scholarship has been published
in the Duke Law Journal, Penn State Law Review, William & Mary Bill of Rights Journal, and UC Law Constitutional Quarterly.  See, e.g., The Broken Branch: Capitalism, the Constitution, and the Press, 125 Penn. St. L.
Rev. 1 (2020); Addiction a nd Expression, 47 Hastings
Const. L.Q. 197 (2020); Doctrinal Dynamism, Borrowing,
and the Relationship Between Rules and Rights (with
Joseph Blocher), 28 Wm. & Mary Bill Rts. J. 319 (2019);
Leave Your Guns at Home: The Constitutionality of a
Prohibition on Carrying Firearms at Political Demonstrations, 68 Duke L.J. 175 (2018).
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
This Court has long prescribed a two-step framework for evaluating constitutional claims.  Step 1 asks
whether the provision invoked applies at all; that is,
whether the challenged regulation or the claimant’s conduct falls within the boundaries of the relevant constitutional guarantee.  Only if so will the court, at the second
step, determine whether the challenged law or regulation passes constitutional muster.  This two-step framework—consisting of “coverage” and “protection,” respectively—applies in some way to nearly all constitutional claims.
  The Second Amendment is no different.  In New
York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1
(2022), this Court adopted a framework under which
courts first ask whether “the Second Amendment’s plain
text covers an individual’s conduct” and, if so, whether
the government has shown, in the face of a presumption
of unconstitutionality, that the challenged regulation “is
consistent with [this] Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”  Id. at 17, 24.  Bruen rejected the

4



means-end scrutiny that the courts of appeals had applied at the second step.  But it described their coverage
analysis—which asked whether regulated conduct fell
“outside the scope of the right as originally understood”—as “broadly consistent with Heller, which demands a test rooted in the Second Amendment’s text, as
informed by history.”  Id. at 18-19 (citation omitted).
Last Term, in United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S. 772
(2026), and Wolford v. Lopez , 609 U.S. 185 (2026), the
Court reiterated the two-step nature of the inquiry.
Wolford restated that first step as involving three “subsidiary questions”: whethe r the challenged regulation
applies to a member of “the people,” whether it concerns
“Arms,” and whether it restricts “keep[ing]” or
“bear[ing].”  609 U.S. at 195 (brackets in original).  Those
questions were not in dispute in Wolford, and the Court
had no occasion to explain how they apply when they are
contested.  They could po tentially be read, however—
and Justice Jackson warned in dissent that they would
be read—to reduce Bruen ’s first step to a mere formality, such that “any law that regulates the carrying of firearms is presumptively unconstitutional.”  609 U.S. at 243
(Jackson, J., dissenting).  Amici write to explain why the
Court should instead confirm that Bruen’s coverage step
requires what Heller envisioned: a meaningful analysis
into the boundaries of the right that the Second Amendment codified.
The stakes of getting Second Amendment coverage
analysis correct are tremendous.  A coverage step that
does nothing would largely repeat the errors that produced Bruen’s course correction.  Before Bruen, the
courts of appeals routinely assumed , without deciding,
that claimants’ conduct fell within the Second

5



Amendment’s boundaries and proceeded to means-end
scrutiny.  Because the step-one inquiry screened out almost nothing—apart from the regulations that Heller itself appeared to bless—all analysis was shunted into the
second step.  Means-end scrutiny buckled under this
load, with courts sustaining regulations under a form of
intermediate scrutiny that turned out to be overly forgiving.  This Court rejected that approach.  But an
empty first step would place the same pressure on
Bruen’s historical-tradition second step.  Courts could
perceive that they face a choice between invalidating
laws regulating conduct well outside the historically understood boundaries of the right or stretching historical
analogies past their breaking points in order to sustain
those laws.  The first course would turn the Second
Amendment into a vehicle for claims it was never understood or intended to support; the second would water
down its protections.
Nor can a coverage step premised solely on literal
text reliably produce sensible outcomes.  Rather, it risks
being both overinclusive and underinclusive.  Read literally, it will deem presumptively unconstitutional regulations of grenades, explosives, portable nuclear devices,
and handguns with obliterated serial numbers, to name
just a few examples of cases in which it was never
thought problematic for the government to regulate.
From there, courts and litigants will be forced to find
and parse historic analogues to test that presumption.
They may fail to do so, and in so doing either extend the
right to an unreasonable and unanticipated degree or
distort Bruen’s test to avoid such an extension and
thereby undermine its goal of to restraining judicial discretion.  At the same time, a semantically literal test
threatens to be underinclusive, failing to reliably extend

6



the right to protect activity  implicating the core of its
historically understood meaning.  Various laws and regulations that affect firearms—such as those governing
ammunition, acquiring or selling a firearm, or training at
a range—do not implicate th e Amendment’s plain text,
understood as its literal, semantic meaning.  The lower
courts, recognizing as much, have already begun to improvise tests the text does not contain.
There is a better solution.  The Second Amendment
protects “the right of the people to keep and bear
Arms”—a right that, as this Court has explained, the
Amendment “codified” rather than created.  District of
Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008).  The Amendment’s plain text, therefore, refers to a “right” with historically understood boundaries—and identifying those
boundaries is part of reading the text, not a departure
from it.  This Court should take this first post- Wolford
opportunity to confirm that Bruen’s first step requires
meaningful analysis, in which courts determine whether
the people, firearms, and conduct at issue fall within the
right as understood when it was codified, drawing on history that “elucidates how contemporaries understood
the text.”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 213-214 (Barrett, J., concurring) (citation omitted).

7



ARGUMENT
I. This Court’s Individual Rights Precedents Contemplate A First Step That Determines The
Scope Of The Right
A. Constitutional adjudication separates the
scope of a right from the strength of its protection
The adjudication of most constitutional rights claims
begins with a threshold inquiry into their scope.  The
First Amendment, for instance, protects “the freedom of
speech,” but for decades, this Court has recognized categories of expression—obscenity, defamation, incitement, fraud, true threats, and the like—that “lie outside
the bounds of the First Amendment’s protection.”
Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66, 72 (2023).  In the
Fourth Amendment context, the Court has articulated
standards to determine when a government act counts
as a “search” or “seizure,” as  well as to define the “persons, houses, papers, and effects” protected by the
Amendment from such intrusions.  Chatrie v. United
States, 609 U.S. 605, 619-623 (2026)  (citation omitted).
And a criminal defendant’s Sixth Amendment right “to
be confronted with the witnesses against him” has been
construed to reach only statements by those who “bear
testimony.”  Ohio v. Clark, 576 U.S. 237, 243 (2015) (citation omitted).
 These robust coverage tests serve crucial interests
in removing whole categories of unmeritorious claims
from constitutional scruti ny.  Excluding tangential
claims at the threshold ensures that protection of the
constitutional core remains strong.  A right whose every
peripheral claim proceeds to the protection stage is a

8



right whose protection must, sooner or later, be diluted.
See R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul , 505 U.S. 377, 415 (1992)
(Blackmun, J., concurring in judgment) (“If we are forbidden to categorize  * * *  we shall reduce protection
across the board.”).  Categorical threshold rules reduce
the strain on judicial and litigants’ resources.  They also
provide certainty: for the people, who can more easily
understand the legal status of conduct; for regulators,
who can more readily craft rules that meet their constitutional obligations; and for courts, who can rule with
certainty and predictability.  Workable, meaningful coverage tests therefore instrumentally serve the rule of
law.  See Antonin Scalia, The Rule of Law as a Law of
Rules, 56 U. Chi. L. Rev. 1175, 1179 (1989) (“Even in simpler times uncertainty has b een regarded as incompatible with the Rule of Law.”).
B. Heller defined the boundaries of the Second
Amendment right by reference to the historical scope of a pre-existing right
In 2008, this Court held in District of Columbia  v.
Heller that the Second Amendment protects an individual’s right to possess a handgun for self defense, striking
down the District of Columbia’s ban on handgun possession in the home.  554 U.S. 570, 635 (2008).  The Court
observed that the “first salient feature” of the Second
Amendment’s operative clause was that it “codifies a
‘right of the people,’  ” id. at 579, and that “it has always
been widely understood that the Second Amendment,
like the First and Fourth Amendments, codified a preexisting right,” id. at 592.  Thus, the Court looked beyond the plain text to that pre-existing right’s historical
contours to determine what the Amendment protects—
and it found limits.  “Like most rights,” the Court said,

9



“the right secured by the Second Amendment is not unlimited.”  Id. at 626.  Indeed, the Court explicitly referenced the “exceptions” “included” in the pre-existing
right secured by the First Amendment and stated that
“[t]he Second Amendment is no different.”  Id. at 635.
For instance, Heller  explained that “the Second
Amendment does not protect those weapons not typically possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes,” id. at 625, and described that “important limitation on the right to keep and carry arms” as “fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons,’ ” id. at 627 (citation omitted).  It called “startling” a reading of United
States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174 (1939), that would have
cast doubt on federal restrictions on machine guns.  Id.
at 624.  And it described a list of “longstanding”
measures—including prohibitions on possession by felons and the mentally ill, restri ctions in sensitive places,
and “conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale
of arms”—as “presumptively lawful.”  Id. at 626-627 &
n.26.  These statements share a common premise: that
the right’s historical boundaries determine its coverage.
Under Heller, the history is inseparable from the text.
C. Bruen replaced the court of appeals’ second
step, not their first
After Heller, the lower courts developed a two-step
framework.  As the Third Circuit described, the courts
asked “whether the challenged law imposes a burden on
conduct falling within the scope of the Second Amendment’s guarantee.  If it does not, our inquiry is complete.
If it does, we evaluate the law under some form of
means-end scrutiny.  If the law passes muster under that
standard, it is constitutional.”  United States v.

10



Marzzarella, 614 F.3d 85, 89 (2010) (citation omitted);
see New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597
U.S. 1, 17-18 (2022) (describing the framework).  In practice, as Part II explains, the first step often went unperformed.
Bruen rejected the lower courts’ second step, holding that the Court’s precedent “do[es] not support applying means-end scrutiny in the Second Amendment context.”  597 U.S. at 19.  But it affirmed the first step—
under which the government could prevail by showing
that “the challenged law regulates activity falling outside the scope of the right as originally understood”—as
“broadly consistent with Heller, which demands a test
rooted in the Second Amendment’s text, as informed by
history.”  Id. at 18-19 (citation omitted).  Moreover,
Bruen did not cast doubt on Heller’s recognition of categorical limits on the Amendment’s scope.  Two members
of the majority concurred to emphasize as much, see id.
at 80-81 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring), and the majority
made clear that its object was to ensure that the Second
Amendment was not  “subject to an entirely different
body of rules than the other Bill of Rights guarantees,”
id. at 70 (quoting McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S.
742, 780 (2010) (plurality opinion)). In United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680 (2024), the Court focused on clarifying step two of the framew ork because there was no
dispute at step one.  Last Term is when questions over
step one came to the Court.
D. Wolford  restated the first step in textual
terms
In Wolford v. Lopez , the Court reaffirmed that
Bruen’s framework “involves two steps.”  609 U.S. 185,
195 (2026); see also United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S.

11



772, 780 (2026) (describing two steps, with the first focused on “whether the Amendment’s terms cover the
conduct in question”).  The Court described the first step
as a “determin[ation] [of] whether the law  * * *  clashes
with the ‘plain text’ of the Amendment’s language.”
Wolford, 609 U.S. at 195 (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at 24).
It then articulated “three subsidiary questions” to guide
that Step 1 inquiry: “First, does the law apply to ‘the
people’—which is to say, to ‘all members of the political
community’?  Second, does it concern any form of ‘Arms,’
i.e., any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes?  Third, does the law place any restrictions
on either the ‘keep[ing]’ ( i.e., possession) or the
‘bear[ing]’ (i.e., carrying) of arms?”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at
195 (internal citations  omitted)  (brackets in original).
Echoing Bruen, the Court stated that if the claimant’s
conduct implicated all three subsidiary questions, the
challenged law would be deemed “presumptively unconstitutional,” and the government would need to justify it
by reference to regulatory tradition.  Id. at 196.
None of those literal text questions was contested in
Wolford. “No party dispute[d] that petitioners are
among ‘the people’ protected by the Second Amendment
or that they seek to ‘bear,’ i.e., to carry, ‘arms.’ ” 609 U.S.
at 202.  Instead, the state argued that, under background
principles of property law, the right to bear arms did not
include armed entry onto another’s property without the
owner’s consent.  The Court held that argument, which
rested on “historical materials and precedents,” to be
“out of place at Bruen ’s first step,” explaining that at
that step “the question is simply whether a challenged
law falls within the Second Amendment’s ‘plain text.’  ”
Id. at 204-205 (citation omitted).  As such, the Court had

12



no occasion to explain how courts should analyze a contested coverage question.
Wolford did, however, preserve Heller and Bruen’s
insistence that history gives text its meaning.  The definitions at the heart of the “subsidiary questions”—“the
people” as members of the political community, “Arms”
as weapons customarily used for offense or defense, and
“keep” and “bear” as possess and carry—are drawn from
Heller’s analysis of the Amendment’s originally understood meaning.  Heller, 554 U.S. at 579-592.  The Wolford
Court likewise reaffirmed th e theoretical foundation of
resort to history, reiterating that the Amendment “codified a pre-existing right,” Wolford, 609 U.S. at 193 (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 592), and that the right is subject
to “important limitation[s],” Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.  Justice Barrett, concurring, explained that courts at the
first step must “look to history that ‘elucidates how contemporaries understood the text.’ ”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at
213-214 (Barrett, J., concurring).
Wolford’s restatement could, however, be read more
broadly.  Justice Jackson warned in dissent that “the upshot of the majority’s view of Bruen’s first step,” at least
under one reading of it, is “t hat any law that regulates
the carrying of firearms is  presumptively unconstitutional.”  Wolford , 609 U.S. at 243 (Jackson, J., dissenting).  Petitioners and the United States embrace a version of that reading here.  See Pet. Br. 26-28; U.S. Amicus Br. 8-9.  Several courts of appeals, by contrast, have
continued to resolve challenges at the first step since
Wolford.  See United States v.  Berger, 189 F.4th 333,
339-341 (3d Cir. 2026); United States v. DeFelice, No. 25-
920, 2026 WL 2588603 (2d Cir. Sep. 2, 2026) (per curiam);
United States v. Clerfe, 186 F.4th 141, 146 (3d Cir. 2026).

13



II. An Empty First Step Would Repeat The Error
That Produced Bruen  And Distort The Protection
The Second Amendment Affords
Coverage and protection are conceptually distinct,
but in practice they decide cases together.  An analytically defunct threshold places heavier demands on the
step-two inquiry.  The attempts by some theorists to
make First Amendment protection absolute, for example, resulted in a narrow understanding of what counts
as covered speech, for “rights whose coverage is too
broad are likely to offer little in the way of protection.”
Frederick Schauer, Categories and the First Amendment: A Play in Three Acts , 34 Vand. L. Rev. 265, 276
(1981).  The relationship is, in  a word, “hydraulic.”  Joseph Blocher & Eric Ruben, Originalism-by-Analogy
and Second Amendment Adjudication, 133 Yale L.J. 99,
118 (2023).  See Gundy v. United States , 588 U.S. 128,
166-167 (2019) (Gorsuch, J., dissenting) (“When one legal
doctrine becomes unavailable to do its intended work,
the hydraulic pressures of our constitutional system
sometimes shift the responsibility to different doctrines.”).  The history of Second Amendment doctrine in
the lower courts since Heller is largely a history of that
dynamic. See Luke Smith Morgan, The Second Amendment After Doctrine (forthcoming 2027),  https://dx.doi.
org/10.2139/ssrn.7286538.
A. Before Bruen, assumed coverage distorted
the protection inquiry
While the lower courts after Heller correctly
erected a recognizable two-step framework, they did not
employ a particularly scrutinizing first step.  Instead,
many treated Heller’s  acknowledgment of “longstanding” and “presumptively lawful” regulations, 554 U.S. at

14



626-627 & n.26, as a litmus test, presuming that any regulations that overlapped with these areas were lawful
(thus ending their analysis).  As the Third Circuit observed, many federal appellate courts “characterized the
‘presumptively lawful’ language in Heller as dicta,” but
“[e]ven so, these courts relied on the Heller ‘dicta’ to reaffirm the constitutionality” of challenged laws.  United
States v. Barton, 633 F.3d 168, 171 (2011).  More often,
courts simply assumed without deciding that the challenged law governed conduct that implicated the Second
Amendment right and proceeded to means-end scrutiny.
See, e.g., Kanter v. Barr, 919 F.3d 437, 447 n.9 (7th Cir.
2019) (referring to “defer[ring] the threshold historical
scope inquiry and proceed[i ng] directly to means-end
scrutiny” as the “ ‘prudential approach’ ”); United States
v. Masciandaro, 638 F.3d 458, 474 (4th Cir. 2011) (“[I]t
is unnecessary to explore  * * *  the question of whether
and to what extent the Second Amendment right recognized in Heller applies outside the home.”).
As a consequence, means-end scrutiny had to carry
the entire weight of Second Amendment adjudication,
whether that adjudication involved claims at the right’s
periphery or at its core.  To sustain regulations that no
one seriously considered unconstitutional, courts applied
a weak version of intermediate scrutiny.  That deference, however, did not stay at the periphery.  In Professor Joseph Blocher and Eric Ruben’s statistical analysis
of post-Heller cases, courts selected intermediate scrutiny 79 percent of the time, and those claims had a 10
percent success rate.  Eric Ruben & Joseph Blocher,
From Theory to Doctrine: An Empirical Analysis of the
Right to Keep and Bear Arms After Heller, 67 Duke L.J.
1433, 1496 (2018).  Members of this Court came to view
the result as the treatment of the Second Amendment as

15



“a second-class right.”  Friedman v. City of Highland
Park, 577 U.S. 1039, 1039 (2015) (Thomas, J., dissenting
from the denial of certiorari).  Bruen responded by replacing the second step.  But the deference Bruen condemned was, in significant part, the hydraulic consequence of missing coverage analysis.
B. An empty first step would place the same
pressure on Bruen ’s historical tradition test
If, as Justice Jackson warned, nearly every firearm
regulation conceivable woul d trigger the Amendment’s
coverage under Wolford’s gloss on Bruen’s first step, the
pattern risks repeating itself.  Under such an approach,
most firearm regulations will  arrive at the second step
presumptively unconstitutional, and the government
will bear the burden of ident ifying a historical tradition
that justifies each.
That burden is poorly suited as a blanket rule to be
applied to all firearms regulat ions, even to those that
govern conduct outside the historical right.  When conduct falls outside of the right’s historically understood
boundaries, there will frequently be no regulatory tradition upon which to base an analogy.  The conduct may
have been governed by general property, tort, or criminal law, leaving no firearm-specific footprint, as Wolford
demanded.  It may have been too rare, or too plainly unprotected, to prompt legislat ion.  Or it may have involved technology that did not yet exist.  See Jacob D.
Charles, The Dead Hand of a Silent Past: Bruen, Gun
Rights, and the Shackles of History , 73 Duke L.J. 67
(2023).  Under an empty first step, the government could
lose in the cases it should most readily win.

16



Courts confronting such cases face two likely options, neither optimal.  First, they can invalidate laws
regulating conduct the Second Amendment never protected, simply because they conclude the proffered historical analogues are too far afield—such as for laws
criminalizing the possession of firearms with obliterated
serial numbers.  E.g. , United States v. Price, 635 F.
Supp. 3d 455 (S.D. W. Va. 2022), rev’d, 111 F.4th 392 (4th
Cir. 2024) (en banc).  Or, they could sustain such laws by
reasoning from historical “principles” at ever higher levels of generality, until nearly any modern regulation can
be matched with some historical justification.  In United
States v. Rahimi, this Court correctly recognized that
the historical inquiry does not demand a “historical
twin” and is not “a law trapped in amber.”  602 U.S. 680,
691-692 (2024) (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30).  But, as
Justice Barrett cautioned, “a court must be careful not
to read a principle at such a high level of generality that
it waters down the right.”  Id. at 740 (Barrett, J., concurring).  The more unmeritorious or peripheral cases that
reach the second step, the more generic historical analogies will likely become.  Such is the path means-end scrutiny traveled before Bruen.  An effective coverage doctrine, screening out claims that fall outside of the right’s
historical boundaries, will ensu re that the historical inquiry remains demanding in cases in which it properly
applies.
III. A Purely Textual First Step Would Be Both Overinclusive And Underinclusive
Should Bruen’s coverage step be reduced to the semantic meaning of the Amendment’s literal text, the
three “subsidiary questions” would not merely fail to
screen out claims beyond the right’s boundaries.  They

17



would also work to exclude conduct the right has long
been understood to protect.  The threshold test would
err in both directions, expanding the right beyond the
historical scope codified by the Amendment, but allowing inroads into the core of the right.
A. Overinclusiveness
Explosives, machine guns, and similar military
weapons.  Wolford defined “Arms” as “any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes.”  609
U.S. at 195.  Read literally, that description reaches grenades, rocket launchers, machine guns, and other explosive devices.  Before and after Bruen, the courts of appeals consistently rejected Second Amendment challenges to restrictions on such weapons.  See, e.g., United
States v. Morgan, 150 F.4th 1339 (10th Cir. 2025); United
States v. Tagg, 572 F.3d 1320 (11th Cir. 2009); United
States v. McCartney, 357 F. App’x 73 (9th Cir. 2009) (unpublished); United States v.  Fincher, 538 F.3d 868 (8th
Cir. 2008); see also United States v. Ocker-Mullen, No.
20-cr-00313, 2024 WL 2834845, at *4 (M.D. Pa. June 4,
2024) (grenades).  However, under a literalist first step,
such restrictions would be presumptively unconstitutional.  Their ultimate validity would depend on the government’s success in finding a historical analogue, even
as Heller itself described as “startling” a reading of precedent that would have cast doubt on federal restrictions
on machine guns.  554 U.S. at 624.  Some judges have
read Wolford’s language more narrowly, reasoning that
the “offensive or defensive purposes” it contemplates do
not include uses best suited to military force.  Association of N.J. Rifle & Pistol Clubs, Inc. v. Attorney Gen.
N.J., 183 F.4th 211, 285 n.8 (3d Cir. 2026) (emphasis
added) (Shwartz, J., dissenting) .   In so doing, they

18



understand the text by reference to the historical purposes of the right the text codified—exactly what a
meaningful first step requires.
The problem does not stop at conventional weapons.
The Seventh Circuit has observed that, without a meaningful threshold inquiry, even “a nuclear weapon such as
the now-retired M388 Davy Crockett system, with its
51-pound W54 warhead,” would fall within the Amendment’s literal text.  Bevis v. City of Naperville, 85 F.4th
1175, 1182 (7th Cir. 2023).  The United States has declined to foreclose that possibility.  See Br. for the
United States as Amicus Curiae at 12, Granata v. Campbell, No. 25-1918 (1st Cir. Jan. 28, 2026).  Its answer in
this case is not a constitutional principle but an assurance about demand.  See U.S. Amicus Br. 17-18.
Untraceable firearms.  The problem is not confined
to exotic weapons.  Federal law prohibits possessing a
firearm whose serial number has been removed, obliterated, or altered.  18 U.S.C. 922(k).  As some lower court
judges have concluded, a handgun with a defaced serial
number is still a weapon customarily used for defensive
purposes, and possessing one is “keeping” it.  United
States v. Price, 111 F.4th 392, 426 (4th Cir. 2024) (Richardson, J., dissenting).  Under a literal first step, Section 922(k) would be presumptively unconstitutional.
And, as Judge Richardson’s dissent in Price indicates, it
may be difficult for the government to identify appropriate analogues, regardless of whether there is any reason
to believe that the right as historically understood would
preclude the government from enacting such a law.
Committing a Crime of Violence .  Nor is the problem confined to weaponry.  A literal-text-only first step
could render presumptively unconstitutional laws that

19



no one contends raise any constitutional concern whatsoever.  Federal law provides mandatory imprisonment
for one who “carries a firearm” “during and in relation to
any crime of violence or drug trafficking crime” or even
“possesses a firearm” in further ance of those activities.
18 U.S.C. 924.  But if Wolford is read to reduce step one
to a dictionary checklist of “people,” “arms” and “keep or
bear,” then the bank robber charged under 924(c) has a
cognizable claim that punishing his bearing of a handgun
is presumptively unconstitutional.  Cf.  United States v.
Green, No. 25-50841, 2026 WL 2790680, at *1 (5th Cir.
Sep. 17, 2026) (“The Supreme Court has not issued a
post-Bruen opinion addressing whether or how § 924(c)
implicates the Second Amendment.”).  The fact that such
a claim would fail at step two is besides the point. It
should not even get through the door because using a
gun to rob a bank is far outside the historically understood scope of the preexisting right enshrined in the Second Amendment.  See, e.g., United States v. Risner, 129
F.4th 361, 368 (6th Cir. 2025)  (reaffirming prior circuit
precedent concluding that “the historical understanding
of the right to keep and bear arms does not extend to the
use of a firearm for an unlawful purpose”).
B. Underinclusiveness
The same literalism that admits too much also excludes too much.  Wolford described “keep[ing]” as “possession” and “bear[ing]” as “c arrying.”  609 U.S. at 195
(brackets in original).  Many laws that burden the right
regulate neither.
Acquisition and ammunition.  As courts have frequently acknowledged, the right to keep and bear arms
would mean little if the government could freely prohibit
acquiring arms or the amm unition necessary to use

20



them.  E.g., Jackson v. City & County of San Francisco,
746 F.3d 953, 967 (9th Cir. 2014) (“[W]ithout bullets, the
right to bear arms would be meaningless.”).  But a person seeking to buy a firearm does not yet “possess” one.
Nor does a restriction on purchasing ammunition, in the
narrowest sense, regulate the possession or carrying of
an “Arm.”  A textually literal first step thereby would
seem to permit inroads on the core of the right.  For example, in United States v. Clerfe, the Third Circuit held
that a conviction for arms trafficking did not implicate
the Second Amendment because the defendant’s conduct “involved dispossessing himself of firearms,” and
“[r]eading ‘keep Arms’ to include ‘giving away Arms’
would conflict with the most basic rule of constitutional
interpretation.”  186 F.4th 141, 146 (2026).  Amici do not
disagree with the Third Circuit that arms trafficking
should not be covered by the Second Amendment, but
note that the court’s textually literal reading applies
with equal force to the conventional sale of weapons to
qualified purchasers within the United States.
Training and proficiency.   Heller recognized that,
as historically understood, “t o bear arms implies something more than the mere keeping; it implies the learning to handle and use them in a way that makes those
who keep them ready for their efficient use.”  554 U.S. at
617-618 (quoting Thomas M. Cooley, General Principles
of Constitutional Law in the United States of America
271 (1880)).  The Seventh Circuit accordingly held that a
municipal ban on firing ranges implicated the Second
Amendment, reasoning that “[t]he right to possess firearms for protection implies a corresponding right to acquire and maintain proficiency in their use.”  Ezell v.
City of Chicago , 651 F.3d 684, 704 (2011).  Firing a
weapon at a range is neither possessing nor carrying it.

21



So, a first step that asks only whether a law restricts
possession or carrying would exclude conduct that Heller itself understood the right to include.
C. The lower courts are already (or still) improvising beyond the text
Confronted with these challenges, the courts of appeals have begun devising their own divergent approaches.  The Fifth Circuit has treated restrictions on
purchasing firearms as restrictions on keeping and bearing them.  Elite Precision Customs, LLC v. Bureau of
Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, No. 25-11206,
2026 WL 2796983 (Sep. 18, 2026).  In so doing, the court
explicitly departed from the text, writing that “it is well
established in the American legal tradition that the right
to keep firearms logically entails the right to purchase
them as well.”  Id. at *3.  The Second Circuit, on the
other hand, has held that restrictions on purchasing and
selling arms fall within the text only if they “meaningfully constrain” the underlying right to keep and bear
arms, DeFelice, 2026 WL 2588603, at *4, again supplying
a test not found in the Amendment’s “plain text,”  id. at
*3.  That lower courts are finding it impossible to answer
coverage questions without departing from the plain
text suggests the necessity of clarifying Wolford.
IV. This Court Should Clarify That The First Step
Asks What The Codified Right Encompasses
The Court need not depart from Bruen or Wolford
to correct these problems.  It need only confirm, consistent with those decisions, that the “plain text” of the
Second Amendment refers to a pre-existing right, such
that coverage requires attention to how that right was
understood when codified by the Amendment.

22



Amici agree that the first step begins with the text.
See Food & Drug Admin. v. Alliance for Hippocratic
Med., 602 U.S. 367, 378 (2024) (“ Therefore, we begin as
always with the precise text of the Constitution.”).  The
risk is instead that lower courts may stop at the text, and
divorce that text from its historical context.  The Second
Amendment does not protect “keep[ing] and bear[ing]
Arms” in the abstract.  It protects “the right of the people
to keep and bear Arms,” and provides that this right
“shall not be infringed.”  This  text identifies the object
of the Amendment’s protection as an existing right,
bounded as that right then was.  Or, as Heller  put it,
“[t]he very text of th e Second Amendment implicitly
recognizes the pre-existence of the right and declares
only that it ‘shall not be infringed.’ ”  554 U.S. at 592.  One
cannot conduct a “plain text” analysis without inquiring
into the historically understood dimensions of that right.
See, e.g., Wolford, 609 U.S. at 213-214 (Barrett, J., concurring); Bruen, 597 U.S. at 25 (“[R]eliance on history to
inform the meaning of constitutional text—especially
text meant to codify a pre-existing right—is, in our view,
more legitimate” than other approaches).
This approach does not require courts to abandon
textual fidelity or to import their own policy judgments.
Rather, it conforms to the ordinary methodology of construing constitutional language: ask what the words
meant to those who ratified them in order to determine
the meaning of the right the Amendment codified.  That
is the inquiry Justice Barrett described—one that looks
to “history that ‘elucida tes how contemporaries understood the text.’ ”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 213-214 (Barrett,
J., concurring) (citation omitted).

23



The Court should confirm that the first step of the
Bruen framework requires a meaningful inquiry into
whether the people, arms, and conduct at issue fall
within the right the Second Amendment codified, informed by the historical understanding of that right.
Such a holding would align the Second Amendment with
every other guarantee in the Bill of Rights, rather than
subjecting it to “an entirely different body of rules.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 70 (quoting McDonald, 561 U.S. at
780 (plurality opinion)).  Conducting a robust historical
analysis to determine the scope of a right is not new; as
noted, this historical inquiry has informed the boundaries of many other constitutional rights.  Courts ask
whether the place or item searched falls within the
Fourth Amendment’s scope, whether a statement is testimonial before applying th e Confrontation Clause, and
whether a person is in custody before the Fifth Amendment privilege attaches—“despite no mention of custody in the ‘plain text’ of the Amendment.”  Bevis, 85
F.4th at 1194 (citing New York v. Quarles, 467 U.S. 649,
654 (1984)).  In each instance, coverage turns on the
words as understood against the legal tradition  they
codified.  Therefore, a historically informed “search for
the correct meaning of ‘Arms’ for the Second Amendment is consistent with our approach to its companions
in the Bill of Rights.”  Ibid.
This approach would also keep faith with Heller,
Bruen, and Wolford.  This Court has recognized that
Heller “demands a test rooted in the Second Amendment’s text, as informed by history,” Bruen, 597 U.S. at
19, and that Heller relied on “text and history” in “suggesting the outer limits of the right,” id. at 22.  Bruen,
too, contemplated using history “to determine which
modern ‘arms’ are protected.”  Id. at 28.  And Wolford

24



acknowledged that the right contains historical limits
“not in every way coterminous with the Amendment’s
literal language.”  609 U.S. at 196.  Thus, as Justice Barrett suggested, courts must “look to history that ‘elucidates how contemporaries understood the text’  ” at
Bruen’s first step.  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 213-214 (Barrett,
J., concurring) (citation omitted).
Finally, reaffirming that the Second Amendment requires a meaningful coverage step would protect the
right itself, by reserving the demanding historical inquiry Bruen prescribed for the claims to which it was
meant to apply.
CONCLUSION
The Court should reaffirm a two-step methodology
for adjudicating Second Amendment claims that
includes a meaningful first step that properly
encapsulates the scope of the pre-existing right that the
Second Amendment protects.
